chapter_theme: Poems 181-200 are mostly maxims on what keeps the world, a land, a king and a life worth while: the selfless, learning above birth, measured levies, good men, giving, steady friends and equanimity before fate. They end with bards' poems on asking and giving that test those maxims on real patrons.

181.reading: A poet sends a hungry bard straight to Pannan, the true-sworded lord of a harsh, fenced forest country, telling him to go at once and show his hunger before Pannan rides out to enemy land.
181.nuance: The opening picture of the hunters' settlement, where the woman's son and a forest elephant's calf go after the same fallen wood-apple, is both a sign of a wild, unploughed land and of a lord whose people live without fear; the urgency of இன்னே and the timing clause (before he goes to the enemy's land) make the patron's generosity a thing that can be missed. Who takes the fruit in lines 1 to 3 is not certain from the syntax.

thinai_evidence.note: the act of the poem is directing a starving bard to a giver, which is guide-poem praise, though the colophon files it under valour

182.reading: The world goes on only because there are people who would not eat even the gods' nectar alone, who are without anger or sloth, fear what others fear, give their lives for honour and refuse the whole world if it comes with blame, and strive not for themselves but for others.
182.nuance: The poem is a single sentence that holds its subject back to the last line: the list of refusals comes first and only then does it say who these people are. The poet is a Pandya prince, so the claim that the world rests on the selfless comes from a ruler, not a supplicant.

thinai_evidence.note: a general truth about what sustains the world, addressed to no one

183.reading: Learning is good even at the cost of serving and paying the teacher and not resenting the lower place: a mother's heart leans to the more accomplished of her own children, a king takes counsel from the wise brother rather than the eldest, and when a man of the lowest of the four orders learns, a man of the highest comes to him.
183.nuance: Three hierarchies are tested in turn, the family, the royal house and the four orders, and in each learning wins over birth order or birth rank. The poet is a king, Nedunchezhiyan, so the poem concedes that even the throne's counsel follows learning. The hierarchies are named, not abolished.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises learning as an excellence that overturns rank, the kind of praise of a calling the Tholkappiyam puts under vaakai

184.reading: If a king takes his due as an elephant is fed ripe paddy cut into balls, even a small field lasts many days and the country thrives, but if a weak king with a noisy, unruly retinue grabs what he can, he is like an elephant let loose in a field that tramples more than it eats: he goes hungry and the land is ruined.
184.nuance: The argument is made to the king's own interest, not the subject's: greed leaves the king himself unfed (தானும் உண்ணான்). The blame falls partly on the retinue that does not know order (வரிசை அறியா), so the weak king is the one who cannot restrain those around him.

thinai_evidence.note: counsel spoken to a king, the admonition the Tholkappiyam counts under praise

comparisons.tenor: the wise king who levies by measure
the realm stripped by a greedy king and his retinue

185.reading: The realm is a cart of protection running on wheel and axle: if its driver is skilled it goes smoothly without harm, but if he cannot steer it sinks daily in the mire of enmity and brings one great evil after another.
185.nuance: The poet is himself a king, Tondaiman Ilandiraiyan, so the image of the incompetent driver is a ruler's self-warning. The cart is protection (காவல்), not wealth or conquest: the realm exists to guard.

thinai_evidence.note: a general maxim about rule, spoken by a king and addressed to no one

comparisons.tenor: the kingdom and its government
the troubles that enmity brings on a realm

186.reading: Rice is not life and water is not life: the wide world lives by its king, so it is the duty of the king with a spear-strong army to know that he is its life.
186.nuance: The last clause turns praise into duty: it is not the people who must know the king is their life, but the king who must know it (அறிகை ... கடனே). Read that way, the poem binds the king rather than flattering him.

thinai_evidence.note: a statement of what the king is to the world, addressed to no hearer

187.reading: Be it settled country or forest, low ground or high, a land is good only where its men are good; bless you, land.
187.nuance: Avvaiyar names four kinds of ground, the very terms by which land is classed, only to declare them irrelevant; the landscape that orders all Sangam poetry is set aside in four short lines. The goodness is the men's, and the land is praised for reflecting it.

thinai_evidence.note: a maxim on what makes a land good, addressed to the land itself

188.reading: However rich a man is, with many dishes and many guests, if he has no little children who toddle up, stretch out small hands, put in, touch, bite and stir the food and scatter the ghee rice over themselves, his days of living bring him no profit.
188.nuance: The four verbs of line 4 are a child's whole repertoire with food, and the poem lingers on the mess before it gives its verdict. The poet is the Pandya king Arivudai Nambi, a man of the feasting wealth he says is worthless without children.

thinai_evidence.note: a general verdict on what makes a life fruitful

189.reading: Whether he is the sole king under the white umbrella of the sea-girt earth or an unlettered hunter who watches for game sleepless at midnight and by day, each eats one measure and wears two cloths, and all else is the same; so the use of wealth is giving, for whoever means to enjoy it all himself loses much.
189.nuance: The argument is from the body's limit, not from virtue or merit: a stomach takes one naazhi whatever one owns, so surplus can only be given or lost. The final line can be read either as the hoarder failing in many duties or as many things slipping from his grasp.

thinai_evidence.note: a maxim on the use of wealth, addressed to no one

190.reading: Let me have no friendship with the small-hearted who, like the rat that eyes a little field at harvest and stuffs its hole with curved ears of grain, only build up what they already have; let my days be joined with the strong-hearted, unflagging as the hungry tiger that will not eat a boar fallen on its left side and next day rises from its cave to bring down a great bull elephant.
190.nuance: The two similes are built as opposites of scale: the rat fills its hole from a small field, the tiger refuses an easy boar and hunts an elephant. The tiger's refusal of prey fallen on the left is an omen custom, and it makes the tiger's hunger a chosen one.

thinai_evidence.note: a wish about the choice of friends, a general matter

comparisons.tenor: those who only hoard what they already have
the strong-hearted who will not stoop and aim high

191.reading: Asked why he has no grey hair after so many years, the poet answers that his wife is excellent, his children grown, his servants of one mind with him, the king does no wrong and protects, and above all his town has many worthy men, full in learning, calm and restrained.
191.nuance: The answer moves outward in rings: wife, children, servants, king, and last the worthy men of the town, which the poet sets above all (அதன்தலை). Freedom from age is credited to the people one lives among, not to diet, discipline or renunciation.

thinai_evidence.note: a general account of the good life, answered to an imagined questioner

192.reading: Every town is ours and everyone our kin; good and ill do not come from others, nor do pain and its easing; death is nothing new, and we neither rejoice that life is sweet nor in disgust call it bitter, for we have seen through the wise that a life moves by its order like a raft carried down a great river roaring over rocks after the lightning and rain, so we do not marvel at the great and still less despise the small.
192.nuance: The famous first line is the conclusion of an argument, not a slogan: because good and ill are not given by others, no place is foreign and no one a stranger. The raft image keeps the agent out of view; the poem says a life follows its course (முறைவழி) but does not name who set it. The equanimity is learnt from the wise (திறவோர் காட்சியின்), not claimed as one's own discovery.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is about meeting life and death in a world that does not stay

comparisons.tenor: a life that follows its order

193.reading: Like an antelope chased by one man across a long white salt plain spread like a flayed hide, one might run and escape, but the life of a household binds the legs.
193.nuance: The poet's name, the one-plough farmer, is taken from the poem's world, and the four lines leave unsaid what he would flee: the chase is from his troubles, and the household is both what makes him want to run and what keeps him from it.

thinai_evidence.note: a general complaint about the bonds of household life

comparisons.tenor: the wide, bare white salt plain
the man who might flee his troubles

194.reading: In one house the dirge drum sounds, in another the cool wedding drum throbs; the joined wear flowers while the parted weep from kohl-lined eyes: whoever made this world is surely without kindness. This world is harsh; let those who know its nature look for what is sweet.
194.nuance: நெய்தல் here is the drum or tune of mourning, not the shore landscape or the flower. The poem blames the maker (படைத்தோன்) outright, which is rare, and then turns from complaint to counsel: knowing the world is harsh is the ground for seeking good (இனிய), not for leaving it.

thinai_evidence.note: the world's harshness and the passing of joy into grief

195.reading: You many worthies with hair grey as fish bones and wrinkled cheeks, in useless old age, you will grieve when the fierce one with the sharp axe binds you: if you cannot do good, at least keep from doing harm, for that pleases everyone and is also the road to the good way.
195.nuance: The address பல்சான்றீரே, repeated three times, is ironic: the 'many worthies' have reached old age without doing good. Death is not named but drawn as one who carries a கணிச்சி, an axe. The advice sets a floor, not a summit: refraining from harm is offered as already a way to the good.

thinai_evidence.note: old age and death held up to the living, the theme the Tholkappiyam gives to kaanchi

comparisons.tenor: the old men's grey hair

196.reading: To say yes to what one can give and no to what one cannot are both proper ways of a giver's friendship, but to promise what one cannot and refuse what one can both wound the asker and lessen the giver's fame; I have seen it now, so may your sons be well, and I, not shrinking from sun or dew, will go home to my poor shelter thinking of my faithful, bright-browed wife.
196.nuance: The rebuke is framed as a general rule of four cases before it becomes personal, and the poet's parting blessing on the king's sons keeps the rebuke from becoming a curse. The sense of கல்குயின்றன்ன, describing his shelter, is not secure.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem speaks to a patron about how a giver must answer a suppliant

comparisons.tenor: the poet's poor shelter from the wind

197.reading: We do not marvel at the white-umbrella wealth of kings with wind-swift horses, bannered chariots, sea-wide armies, hill-rivalling elephants and thunder-loud drums; we marvel at small-village chiefs who, though they eat only greens and varagu rice, know how to treat us; we think nothing of the riches of the unfeeling, and think of the poverty of the wise with great joy, lord.
197.nuance: Spoken to a great Chola king, the poem is a refusal and a warning in the form of praise of others: the grand catalogue of lines 1 to 8 is built up only to be dismissed. The small chief's meal is described with care (greens the goats have left, millet from dry land), and the point is that he knows the poet's worth (பாடறிந்து).

thinai_evidence.note: a poet speaks to a king about whom poets honour

comparisons.tenor: the kings' swift horses
the kings' vast armies
the kings' elephants
the kings' war drums

198.reading: Having blessed the king's sons, born of his chaste, god-like queen, and seen his wealth, like that of the god under the banyan, the poet takes leave wishing the sons to be like their ancestors who filled the palace with enemies' treasure, and the king to live on, his days more than the sea's water, its sand and the sky's rain, while the poet in his distant land, like the bird that longs for a raindrop, waits for his grace: 'Maran, do not forget me.'
198.nuance: The poem is a leave-taking, not a thanks: the poet says his heart, which cries out even in dreams for lack of the king's favour, rejoiced in seeing his wealth (ஏமாந்து உவப்ப), and his last words ask not to be forgotten, so the gift is still awaited. The bird that lives on raindrops makes his waiting a matter of nature, not of choice.

thinai_evidence.note: praise and blessing of a king by a departing poet

comparisons.tenor: the king's garlanded chest
the children's mouths
the king's wealth
the king's sons, like him in might
the king's sons, who should be as their ancestors

comparisons.vehicle: பெருங்கடல் நீரினும், அக்கடல் மணலினும், நீண்டுஉயர் வானத்து உறையினும்
comparisons.tenor: the king's years
the poet longing for the king's grace

199.reading: A noisy flock of birds does not say 'we ate yesterday' but keeps returning to the many fruits of the wide-branched banyan where a god dwells; so are suppliants, and the wealth of the generous men who welcome them is the suppliants' wealth, their want the suppliants' want.
199.nuance: The poem defends the suppliant's repeated asking by nature: birds do not count yesterday's meal. The last two lines join giver and asker in one fortune, so the patron's poverty would be the poet's poverty too; asking is made a bond, not a debt.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of givers through the conduct of suppliants

comparisons.tenor: suppliants who return to a patron without shame

200.reading: Kapilar addresses Vichikko, lord of high hills where monkeys feast on jackfruit and sleep on bamboo, a king with a fat-eating spear and fierce elephants: these are the daughters of Pari, who gave his tall belled chariot to a jasmine creeper though it never sang for him; I am a suppliant and a brahmin; take them as I give them, lord of a land of unfailing harvests.
200.nuance: The bard offers the daughters as a gift he himself makes (கொடுப்பக் கொண்மதி), claiming the standing of brahmin and suppliant. Pari's gift to the jasmine is invoked to show what kind of father the girls had, generous even to a creeper that could not praise him. The monkey and his mate in the hill-description may be read as a hint at the marriage proposed, but nothing in the poem states it, so it is left as scene.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard addresses a king, praising him and his dead patron

links.note: Both say the world stands because of a certain kind of person: 182 names those who strive for others, Kural 996 those of courtesy (பண்புடையார்), without whom it would sink into the earth.
links.teaches: The Kural compresses into a two-line rule what the Pandya prince builds as a list of concrete refusals, so the reader of the Kural can see which deeds (not eating alone, dying for honour, refusing blame-tainted gain) its abstract பண்பு was taken to mean.

links.note: 182 opens its catalogue with not eating alone even the nectar of the gods; Kural 322 makes sharing one's food the chief of all virtues.
links.teaches: Sharing food heads the list in both books, which shows that in early Tamil ethics the shared meal, not an inner disposition, was the first test of a good person.

links.note: 182 opens உண்டால் அம்ம, இவ்வுலகம் (the world exists, indeed) and 194 says இன்னாது அம்ம, இவ் வுலகம் (the world is harsh, indeed): the same exclamation over the same world.
links.teaches: Two poets use one formula to say opposite things about this world, and each turns it to action, so the formula shows the anthology arguing with itself: the world is kept going by the selfless in 182, and is bitter yet must be met by seeking good in 194.

links.note: Both rank learning above birth: in 183 a man of the highest order defers to a learned man of the lowest, and Kural 409 says the unlearned high-born lack the worth of the learned low-born.
links.teaches: The Kural's maxim was already a king's teaching in the Purananuru, where Nedunchezhiyan keeps the four orders by name and lets learning reverse them, so neither text abolishes birth rank: both use it as the measure that learning overturns.

links.note: Kural 69 has the mother rejoice when her son is called worthy; 183 has the mother's heart turn toward the accomplished child among children of one womb.
links.teaches: Where the Kural shows a mother's joy at one son's public praise, the Purananuru admits the harder consequence, that learning makes her favour one child over his brothers, so the pair shows that the honour of learning reorders even family love.

links.note: Kural 552 calls the sceptre-holder's demand a robber's demand at spear-point; 184 likens the greedy king to an elephant loose in a field.
links.teaches: The Kural condemns excess levy from the subject's side as robbery, while Pisirandhaiyar argues from the king's side that grabbing wastes more than it yields and leaves the king himself unfed, so the same rule is given both a moral and a prudential ground.

links.note: Kural 542 sets the world's dependence on the sky beside the people's dependence on the sceptre; 186 denies rice and water the name of life and gives it to the king alone.
links.teaches: The Kural keeps rain and rule as parallel supports, but Mosikeeranar ranks the king above food and water and then turns the claim into the king's own duty to know it, so the pair shows the same dependence read once as praise and once as a burden laid on the ruler.

links.note: Kural 737 defines a country by its limbs: waters, a well-placed hill, the water from it and a strong fort. 187 says no kind of ground, plain, forest, low or high, makes a land good, only the goodness of its men. On the reading that both answer what makes a land good, they disagree.
links.teaches: The Kural's chapter on the land lists natural and built assets, while Avvaiyar dismisses terrain altogether, so a reader sees two answers to one question, resources or people, and that the Purananuru gave the moral answer before the treatise gave the material one.

links.note: 186 says the world lives by its king; 187 says a land is good wherever its men are good, naming no king.
links.teaches: Placed side by side in the anthology, the two maxims locate the source of a land's well-being in different hands, the ruler in 186 and the men at large in 187, so the reader sees that Sangam counsel did not rest the realm on the king alone.

links.note: Both turn on a small child's hand in the food: Kural 64 says gruel stirred by children's small hands is sweeter than nectar; 188 lists the child's touching, biting, stirring and scattering of ghee rice.
links.teaches: The Kural makes the image a measure of sweetness, while the Pandya king makes its absence a verdict that a rich man's feasting life is profitless, so one scene serves as delight in one book and as the test of a wasted life in the other.

links.note: 189 says the use of wealth is giving and whoever means to enjoy it alone loses much; Naladiyar 9 says the man who neither eats, gives nor relieves his kin but guards his wealth is counted as one who has lost it.
links.teaches: Both declare kept wealth already lost, but for different reasons: Nakkeerar from the fixed measure one body can eat and wear, the Naladiyar from the miser's failure in every use, so the pair gives the conclusion one ground in the body and one in duty.

links.note: Both use the tiger that will not eat prey that has fallen on its left side and goes hungry instead.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar uses the tiger's refusal as a model of one's own honour, while the Chola poet uses it to choose whom to befriend, so the image was a shared emblem of high-mindedness that each book bent to its own question.

links.note: Naladiyar 11 says the wise, knowing grey hair will come, renounced in childhood; 191 says grey hair has not come to the poet because of his good wife, children, servants, king and the worthy men of his town. On the reading that both speak of how to meet old age, one counsels leaving the household and the other credits it.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar's answer to ageing is renunciation, while Pisirandhaiyar's is a good household and good company, so the pair shows two Tamil remedies for the same fear, one by leaving the world early and one by living well in it.

links.note: Kural 379 asks why those who accept good when it comes grieve when it does not; 192 neither rejoices that life is sweet nor calls it bitter, because a life follows its order.
links.teaches: Both ground equanimity on an order the person does not control, but the Kural names it ஊழ் and argues, while Kaniyan gives the picture of a raft carried on a flood, so the abstract fate of the Kural is given an image of how it works.

links.note: Kural 397 says every land and town becomes one's own, and asks why anyone stays unlearned; 192 says every town is ours and everyone our kin, with no condition of learning.
links.teaches: The Kural makes belonging everywhere a reward of learning, while Kaniyan makes it a consequence of seeing that good and ill are not given by others, so the pair shows the same cosmopolitan claim earned once by study and once by insight.

links.note: 194 declares இன்னாது அம்ம, இவ் வுலகம், this world is harsh, and blames its maker; 192 says we do not in disgust call life bitter (இன்னாது என்றலும் இலமே). Read as judgments of the world, they are incompatible.
links.teaches: One anthology holds both the verdict that the world is bitter and the refusal to pass that verdict, using the same word இன்னாது, so the reader sees that Purananuru ethics offered two stances to grief, protest and equanimity, rather than one doctrine.

links.note: Both set a wedding drum against a funeral drum. Naladiyar 23 draws the lesson that the worthy hold to the way of escape; 194 tells those who know the world's nature to look for what is sweet (இனிய காண்க). On the reading that இனிய means good deeds in this life, the two conclusions diverge.
links.teaches: The same sight of joy and mourning side by side leads the Naladiyar to renunciation and the Purananuru poet to seeking good within the world, which shows the later didactic book reusing a Sangam image for a different, ascetic conclusion.

links.note: Kural 335 says good deeds must be hurried to before the death rattle stops the tongue; 195, facing old men who have done no good, asks at least that they refrain from harm.
links.teaches: The Kural's urgency assumes one can still act well, while the Purananuru poet sets a floor for those who will not, so the pair shows that early Tamil counsel allowed abstaining from harm to count as a road to the good when doing good had failed.

links.note: Kural 1051 says if those worth asking withhold, the blame is theirs; 196 says a false promise or a false refusal lessens the giver's fame.
links.teaches: The Kural states as a rule that withholding shames the giver, not the asker, and Avur Moolankizhar applies it to a named king's delay, so the rule had been used as a poet's weapon before it became a maxim.

links.note: Kural 1060 says the asker must not be angry; 196, after naming the king's fault, blesses his sons and leaves.
links.teaches: The poet shows how the Kural's demand for an asker without anger can be met without silence: he names the fault plainly and still blesses, so rebuke and the absence of anger are shown to go together.

links.note: Kural 408 says wealth lodged with the unlearned is more painful than the poverty of the good; 197 says the poet thinks nothing of the riches of the unfeeling and thinks of the poverty of the wise with joy.
links.teaches: The Kural's comparison is spoken by a poet to a Chola king's face in the Purananuru, which shows that the maxim's ranking of the wise poor over the ignorant rich was first a bard's claim on his own dignity before a patron.

links.note: 192 ends பெரியோரை வியத்தலும் இலமே, we do not marvel at the great; 197 says the poet does not marvel (வியத்தலோ இலமே) at kings' umbrella wealth but at small chiefs who know how to treat poets.
links.teaches: Kaniyan's refusal to admire the great is a philosophical stance, and Kumaranar turns it into a bard's practice before a king, choosing whom to admire by conduct, so the pair shows a cosmological equanimity becoming a social rule of honour.

links.note: Naladiyar 206 says saltless millet gruel among one's own is sweeter than milk rice from strangers' hands; 197 prizes the small chief's greens and varagu rice given with regard over kings' wealth.
links.teaches: Both value a poor meal for the regard it is given with, but the Naladiyar finds that regard among kin while the Purananuru finds it in a patron who knows a poet's worth, so the pair shows the bard's patron standing where the family stands in the later book.

links.note: 198 has the poet long for the king's grace like the bird that longs for a raindrop; 199 likens suppliants to birds that return daily to a fruiting banyan.
links.teaches: Both poems make the suppliant a bird, but 198's lone bird waits for a drop and begs not to be forgotten, while 199's flock returns without shame to a sure tree, so the pair shows the bard's two postures, anxious waiting and confident return, and what decides between them is the patron.

links.note: Kural 216 likens the wealth of the kindly to a fruit tree ripening in the middle of a town; 199 likens suppliants to birds that return to a fruiting banyan.
links.teaches: The Kural sees the fruiting tree from the owner's side, as wealth placed where all can reach it, while Perumpadhumanaar sees it from the birds' side, as a place to return to daily, so together they give both halves of the gift relation and make the asker's return a sign of the giver's worth.

links.note: In 200 Kapilar offers Pari's daughters to Vichikko as a suppliant and brahmin; in 201 he offers them to Irungovel as their father's friend, naming himself அந்தணன், புலவன்.
links.teaches: Read together, Kapilar's two offers show him grounding the same gift in different claims, his standing as suppliant and brahmin in 200 and his friendship with their father in 201, so the reader sees how a bard, not a kinsman, asserted the right to give a dead patron's daughters.

new_concepts.gloss: the gift a bard seeks from a patron, and the asking for it
new_concepts.label_source: the verses use the word: பரிசில் in 181 line 10, பரிசிலன் in 200 line 13, and the colophons' பரிசில் கடா நிலை

source_issues: 186: the colophon thurai carries a modern editorial sentence after பொருண்மொழிக் காஞ்சி (ending in a stray closing parenthesis); copied exactly as the check requires, but it is not part of the colophon and should be removed from the core record.
200: the colophon thurai reads பரசிற்றுறை, a misprint for பரிசிற்றுறை; corrected in puram_thurai name.
200: text, poet, patron, thinai and thurai are filled from Duraisamy Pillai's edition (show reports FILLED_FROM_DURAISAMY_PILLAI); marked as it stands.
194: poet, thinai and thurai are filled from Duraisamy Pillai's edition.

183 and 187: the review's line table says sangamtamil.com lacks our opening line(s) (183 line 1; 187 lines 1-2). Our line 1 of 183 states the conditions of learning that line 2 completes, and 187's four lines form a complete poem (the four kinds of ground, then the address to the land), so the differences look like line-breaking or omission on the site; all lines are marked.
195 line 1 (பல்சான் றீரே! பல்சான் றீரே!) is flagged as repeated in 246 and 301; it is a formula of address, not a copying error.
198 line 26: வடியுறை looks like அடியுறை (one who dwells at your feet) joined to the preceding word in sandhi; the sense is clear, the spelling is unusual.
